q: 121. If the water table is nearer to the ground surface, an unlined irrigation canal may become useless because .............
explain: A high water table leads to excessive seepage, which triggers waterlogging in the command area (ayacut). This creates stagnant water conditions conducive to mosquito breeding and disease.

q: 122. The optimum kor depth for rice is .............
explain: Kor-depth is the depth of the first watering after sowing. Rice, being a water-intensive crop, requires a higher kor-depth of 19 cm compared to other cereals.

q: 123. Lacey's regime condition will be realized, if .............
options: silt grade in the channel is variable
channel flows in unlimited, incoherent alluvium of the same character as that of transported material
discharge in the channel is variable
silt charge in the channel is variable
explain: True regime is an ideal state where the channel bed and banks are made of the same material that the river is transporting, allowing the channel to adjust its dimensions freely.

q: 124. The optimum kor depth of wheat is .............
explain: Wheat requires less water than rice during its initial growth stage; its standard kor-depth is approximately 13.5 cm (often rounded to 13 cm in exams).

q: 125. The main reason for the silting up of a canal is .............
explain: Silting occurs if the velocity is too low (inadequate slope), if the channel shape isn't balanced for the silt load, or if the head regulator fails to exclude heavy silt at the intake.

q: 126. The full supply level of a canal at its head regulator should be kept .............
options: at the same F.S.L. of parent canal
15 cm below the F.S.L. of parent canal
15 cm above the F.S.L. of parent canal
explain: To ensure a smooth gravity flow into the off-take canal even during slight fluctuations, the F.S.L. of the off-take is typically kept 15 cm to 30 cm lower than the parent canal.

q: 127. The full supply level (F.S.L.) of a gravity canal is .............
options: about 4 to 5 m above the ground level
explain: For gravity irrigation to be effective, the water level in the canal must be slightly higher than the fields it intends to irrigate.

q: 128. The berms formed finally in the canals will serve the purpose of .............
explain: Berms provide a horizontal transition that acts as a cushion for waves, reduces the pressure on the outer banks, and helps the phreatic line stay within the bank section.

q: 129. The difference between the level of the top of the bank and the F.S.L. is known as .............
explain: Freeboard is the safety vertical distance provided to prevent overtopping of the banks due to waves, sudden discharge increases, or wind action.

q: 130. The minimum free board to be provided should be 90 cm if the discharge in the canal is between .............
explain: As discharge increases, the risk of wave height and surge increases. Standards recommend a 0.9m freeboard for discharges in the range of 60 to 150 cumecs.

q: 131. Borrow pits should preferably be taken from the .............
options: field on the left side of the canal
field on the right side of the canal
field on the left as well as right of the canal
central half width of the section of the canal
explain: To minimize land acquisition costs and simplify logistics, soil for canal banks is ideally borrowed from the center of the canal bed itself where it will eventually be underwater.

q: 132. Disposal of excess excavated earth is used to make spoil bank on .............
explain: Spoil banks are constructed on both or either side of the canal when the volume of cutting significantly exceeds the volume of bank filling required.

q: 133. A land is said to be waterlogged if the pores in the soil are saturated within .............
explain: Waterlogging technically occurs when the water table rises to the level where the capillary fringe reaches the root zone, hindering the aeration of the roots.

q: 134. The top of the capillary zone .............
options: lies above the piezometric surface at all points
lies below the piezometric surface at all points
explain: Capillary action pulls water upward against gravity from the water table (piezometric surface), so the top of the capillary zone is always higher than the actual water table.

q: 135. Water logging can be prevented by .............
options: reducing the percolation from canals and water courses
explain: Prevention involves attacking both the 'input' (lining canals to stop seepage) and the 'storage' (pumping water or using drains to lower the table).

q: 136. A canal has a length of L km and the perimeter of its cross-section is P m. The amount required to line the canal, if the cost of lining per sq. m is C, will be .............
explain: Area to be lined = Perimeter (P) x Length (L). Converting L km to meters: $L \times 1000$. Total Cost = $P \times (L \times 1000) \times C = 1000 PLC$.

q: 137. A triangular channel section has side slopes of 1 vertical : z horizontal. If the depth of flow is y, what is the hydraulic depth?
explain: Hydraulic Depth (D) = Area / Top Width. For a triangle: $Area = z y^2$; $Top Width = 2zy$. $D = (zy^2) / (2zy) = y/2$.

q: 138. The most desirable section for a lined canal is .............
options: trapezoidal with rounded corners for large sections
triangular with round bottom for small sections
explain: Rounded corners reduce friction and prevent silt deposition in corners. Trapezoidal is best for large flows, while triangular is efficient for small discharges.

q: 139. The vertical component of the hydrostatic force on an inclined surface is obtained as .............
options: as the weight of water resting on the inclined surface
explain: The vertical force on any submerged surface is equal to the weight of the volume of liquid vertically above that surface extending up to the free surface.

q: 140. The design of a major hydraulic structure founded on a permeable foundation is generally based on .............
explain: Khosla's theory is the most scientifically accurate method as it considers the flow net and actual pressure distribution, unlike the empirical linear creep theories of Bligh or Lane.

q: 141. The purpose of a cross regulator is .............
options: to increase the depth of flow u/s when the main canal is running with low flow
to regulate the flow in the distributaries
explain: A cross regulator is built across the main canal to 'head up' water. This ensures that even when the main canal has low discharge, the water level is high enough to feed an off-taking distributary canal.

q: 142. Bed bars are provided in a canal .............
options: to watch the general behaviour of the canal
explain: Bed bars are masonry or concrete blocks built flush with the design bed level. they serve as permanent reference points to monitor whether the canal is silting or scouring over time.

q: 143. The flow in a canal siphon is .............
explain: In a canal siphon, the canal is taken under a drain. Since the water travels through a barrel below its normal hydraulic gradient, it flows under pipe pressure rather than as an open channel.

q: 144. When a canal and natural drain approach each other at a same elevation, the cross drainage work provided is .............
explain: A level crossing is used when the bed levels of the canal and the drain are nearly the same. The waters are allowed to mix and are then regulated through gates.

q: 145. The uplift pressure on the roof of an inverted siphon will be maximum when .............
explain: The roof of an inverted siphon (where the drain passes under the canal) experiences maximum upward force when the drain is at its High Flood Level (HFL), exerting maximum hydrostatic pressure.

q: 146. The meandering of a river is most likely in .............
explain: In the delta (or alluvial) stage, the river velocity decreases and the bed material is fine. This allows the river to easily erode its banks and deposit silt, creating the characteristic 'S' curves known as meanders.

q: 147. The crest level of a barrage is kept .............
options: almost at the river bed level with large gates
explain: Unlike a weir, a barrage keeps its crest low (near river bed level) to offer less obstruction to floods. The ponding of water is achieved almost entirely by large adjustable gates.

q: 148. The movement of water under or around a structure built on a permeable foundation is called .............
explain: Creep refers specifically to the travel of water along the contact surface between the underside of the structure and the permeable foundation soil.

q: 149. The irrigation with sewage, (instead of natural water) where the disposal of sewage is the prime object is called .............
explain: Broad irrigation is the process of spreading raw or partially treated sewage over large areas of land to simultaneously treat the waste and grow crops.

q: 150. The proportion of silt in water is called .............
explain: Silt charge is the technical term for the concentration of suspended sediment in a stream, usually measured in parts per million (ppm) or grams per liter.

q: 151. Stone pitching, or any other material laid on a sloping face of an earthen bank to maintain its slope or to protect it from erosion is called
explain: Revetment is a facing of stone, concrete units, or slabs built to protect a scarp, the foot of a cliff, or a bank against erosion by wave action or currents.

q: 152. An excavation filled with impervious material to reduce seepage is called
explain: Both cut-off trenches and key trenches are used in dam construction to intercept seepage through pervious foundations by filling a trench with impervious clay or concrete.

q: 153. A weir in which the tail water level is more than the crest level is called
explain: A weir is considered submerged or 'drowned' when the water level on the downstream side (tail water) rises above the elevation of the weir crest.

q: 154. A weir in which the tail water level is less than the crest level is called
explain: In a free-flow (or free) weir, the tail water level is below the crest, allowing the nappe to discharge freely into the air.

q: 155. A fall in which the crest is kept at or near the canal bed without any glacis, is
explain: A trapezoidal notch fall consists of a wall across the canal with one or more notches; it is designed to maintain the depth-discharge relationship without a sloping glacis.

q: 156. The difference in levels between the top of capillary zone and the water table is
explain: The capillary zone exists above the water table due to surface tension pulling water upward; therefore, its top level is higher (positive difference) than the water table level.

q: 157. In Montague type fall
explain: The Montague fall is characterized by a profile following a parabolic curve, which helps in increasing the velocity and ensuring the formation of a hydraulic jump for energy dissipation.

q: 158. The siphon well drop is ideal for
explain: Siphon well drops (or cylinder falls) are economical and efficient specifically for small discharges coupled with high drop heights.

q: 159. In a homogeneous earth dam without d/s horizontal filter, portion of the d/s face through which seepage flow comes out is
options: neither a stream line nor an equipotential line
explain: The discharge face (seepage surface) on the downstream side is neither a flow line (streamline) nor a constant head line (equipotential line).

q: 160. A canal carries a discharge of 5 m³/s with a slope of 1/100. For the same depth of flow its discharge carrying capacity will be doubled by increasing its slope to
explain: According to Manning's formula, $V \propto \sqrt{S}$. To double the discharge ($Q=AV$), the velocity must double, meaning the slope must increase by $2^2 = 4$ times. $(1/100) \times 4 = 1/25$.

q: 161. Crop rotation means
options: not growing any crop during alternate year
growing simultaneously two different crops in alternate rows
growing different crops in successive seasons
explain: Crop rotation is the practice of growing a series of dissimilar or different types of crops in the same area in sequenced seasons to help restore soil fertility.

q: 162. Natural fertility is generally found in
explain: Alluvial soils, formed by river deposits, are rich in minerals and nutrients, making them naturally the most fertile soil type for agriculture.

q: 163. The duty of well water is more than the duty of canal water because
options: well water is less turbid than canal water
well water is used more economically
well water irrigation incurs less conveyance losses
explain: Duty is higher for wells because the water is closer to the field (less loss) and farmers use it sparingly due to the cost/effort of lifting it.

q: 164. Earthquake forces acting on a gravity dam
options: reduce the self weight of the dam
increase the uplift forces on the base of the dam
increase the horizontal water pressure acting on the dam
explain: Earthquakes generate hydrodynamic pressure (Zanger's formula), which acts as an additional horizontal force against the dam face.

q: 165. The source from which the soil is obtained to make up for the difference between the soil required for embankment and the soil available from the canal excavation is known as
explain: When earthwork in cutting is less than earthwork in filling, the extra soil is dug from 'Borrow Pits'.

q: 166. The canal breach may occur when
options: piping takes place through the canal bank
canal banks are over-topped by excess flows
cultivator cut the embankment to derive additional supply
explain: Canal breaches (structural failures of the bank) can be caused by internal erosion (piping), overtopping, or human interference/intentional cuts.

q: 167. Fluming of a canal in the cross-drainage work will
options: reduce the cost of cross drainage work
enable the canal to draw water from drain
explain: Fluming involves contracting the canal width at a structure to reduce the length of the barrel/bridge, thereby saving construction costs.

q: 168. When the length of the body wall of the fall is less than the normal width of the canal, the fall is then called
explain: A fall is 'flumed' when the crest length is narrower than the canal's bed width, usually requiring transitions to prevent turbulence.

q: 169. Which of the following soils has the least permeability
explain: While clay has high porosity, its individual pores are so small that water moves through them very slowly, resulting in the lowest permeability.

q: 170. The proportional weir is also called as
explain: A Sutro weir is a specially shaped weir where the discharge is directly proportional to the head ($Q \propto H$).

q: 171. If m is the average particle size of silt in mm, then the silt factor is proportional to
explain: Lacey's silt factor formula is $f = 1.76\sqrt{m}$, where $m$ is the particle size in mm.

q: 172. In the case of flow over a rectangular suppressed weir, the pressure underneath the nappe will be
explain: In suppressed weirs, air cannot enter the space under the nappe. As water carries away air, a partial vacuum (negative pressure) is created, which can cause the nappe to 'cling'.

q: 173. The slope of the sides of a Cippoletti weir is
explain: A Cippoletti weir is a trapezoidal weir with side slopes of 1 horizontal to 4 vertical, designed to compensate for end contractions.

q: 174. Which of the following is also known as superfluous water?
explain: Gravitational water (or superfluous water) is the water that drains out of the soil under the influence of gravity; it is not available for plant use.

q: 175. According to Khosla's potential flow theory, the undermining of the floor commences at
explain: Failure by piping (undermining) begins at the exit point (tail end) of the structure where the exit gradient is maximum.

q: 176. The degree of sinuosity is the ratio between the
options: meander length and width of meander
meander length and width of river
curved length and straight air distance
explain: Sinuosity is a measure of how much a river meanders; it is calculated as the ratio of the actual channel length (curved) to the shortest axial distance (straight line).

q: 177. The bed of the canal is lowered in the case of
explain: In a canal siphon (also known as a barrel siphon), the canal is taken below the drainage bed by depressing its bed level to allow the water to flow under pressure.

q: 178. In Lanes weighted creep theory the weights proposed for horizontal and vertical creeps are in the ratio of
explain: Lane suggested that horizontal creep is less effective in reducing uplift than vertical creep. He gave a weight of 1/3 to horizontal creep and 1 to vertical creep (3H:1V).

q: 179. The critical hydraulic gradient, according to Khosla's theory, in alluvial soils is approximately
explain: The critical hydraulic gradient ($i_c$) at which soil particles begin to move (boiling) is roughly $(G-1)/(1+e)$, which for most alluvial soils is approximately 1.0.

q: 180. The irrigation is necessary in an area
options: where there is a scanty rainfall
where commercial crops require more water
explain: Irrigation acts as an artificial supplement to ensure crops receive sufficient moisture regardless of natural rainfall patterns or high-demand crop requirements.

q: 181. The irrigation water is said to be unsatisfactory, if it contains
options: chemicals toxic to plants or to persons using plants as food
chemicals which react with the soil to produce unsatisfactory moisture characteristics
bacteria injurious to persons or animals eating plants irrigated with water
explain: Water quality for irrigation is judged by its chemical toxicity, its effect on soil permeability (sodium hazards), and biological safety.

q: 182. Sandy soils with good drainage become impermeable after prolonged use, if it is irrigated with water containing ............. sodium.
explain: High sodium concentration causes soil dispersion. When sodium replaces calcium/magnesium on soil particles, the soil loses its structure and becomes impermeable.

q: 183. For irrigation purposes, the pH value of water should be
explain: The ideal pH for irrigation water is slightly acidic to slightly alkaline. Extremely high or low pH can affect nutrient availability and soil structure.

q: 184. Which of the salt present in water is harmful for cultivation purposes?
explain: Sodium carbonate (Black Alkali) is highly harmful as it reacts with soil to form a hard, impermeable crust and significantly raises soil pH.

q: 185. When an oven-dried sample of soil is kept open in the atmosphere, it absorbs some amount of water. This water is known as
explain: Hygroscopic water is the moisture absorbed from the atmosphere by soil particles; it is held very tightly by molecular forces and is unavailable to plants.

q: 186. A part of water which exists in the porous space of the soil by molecular attraction, is known as
explain: Capillary water is held in the soil's small pores against gravity by surface tension; this is the primary source of water for plant roots.

q: 187. Super-fluous water is a also called
explain: Gravitational water is called superfluous because it is in excess of what the soil can hold at field capacity and drains away rapidly.

q: 188. A useful soil moisture for plant growth is
explain: Only capillary water (the moisture between Field Capacity and Wilting Point) can be easily extracted by the root systems of most crops.

q: 189. The amount of water required to fill up the pore spaces in soil particles by replacing all air held in pore spaces, is known as
explain: At saturation capacity, every single pore in the soil is filled with water, and no air remains in the soil matrix.

q: 190. The moisture content of the soil, after free drainage has removed most of the gravity water, is known is
explain: Field capacity represents the maximum amount of water a soil can hold against gravity, usually reached 2–3 days after heavy rain or irrigation.

q: 191. Available moisture may be defined as the
options: moisture content at permanent wilting point
difference in water content of the soil between field capacity and permanent wilting
explain: Available moisture = Field Capacity – Permanent Wilting Point. This is the reservoir of water that plants can actually use.

q: 192. The field capacity of a soil depends upon
explain: Field capacity is influenced by soil texture (porosity) and the ability of the soil to hold water against gravity (capillary tension).

q: 193. Consumptive use of water by a crop is equal to
options: the depth of water consumed by evaporation
the depth of water consumed by transpiration
the depth of water consumed by evaporation and transpiration during crop growth, including water consumed by accompanying weed growth
explain: Consumptive use (Evapotranspiration) includes the water lost from the soil surface and plant leaves, plus the water required for plant metabolic processes.

q: 194. The consumptive use of water of a crop
options: is measured as the volume of water per unit area
is measured as depth of water on irrigated area
may be supplied partly by precipitation and partly by irrigation
explain: Consumptive use is typically expressed as a depth (e.g., mm/day) and can be met by natural rainfall or supplemental irrigation.

q: 195. The ratio between the area of a crop irrigated and the quantity of water required during its entire period of the growth, is known as
explain: Duty represents the relationship between the volume of water and the area of land it can mature. (Hectares per cumec).

q: 196. The total depth of water required by a crop during the entire period the crop is in the field, is known as
explain: Delta ($\Delta$) is the total depth of water (usually in cm or m) required by a crop to come to maturity.

q: 197. The duty is largest
options: at the head of the main canal
at the head of the water course
explain: Duty increases as we move downstream from the canal head toward the field because conveyance losses are reduced as the measuring point gets closer to the crop.

q: 198. The time (in days) that crop takes from the instant of its sowing to that of harvest, is known as ............. period.
explain: Crop period is the actual biological duration from sowing to harvesting, whereas Base period is the duration from the first to the last watering.

q: 199. The whole period of cultivation from the time when irrigation water is first supplied for preparation of the ground to its last watering before harvesting, is called
explain: Base period ($B$) is used in engineering calculations for duty and delta; it is slightly shorter than the crop period.

q: 200. Crop ratio is the ratio of area irrigated
options: in Rabi season to Kharif season
in Kharif season to Rabi season
under perennial crop to total crop
under perennial crop to non-perennial crop
explain: In irrigation planning, crop ratio is specifically the ratio of the area of Rabi crops to the area of Kharif crops.
